A content delivery network is a system of computers spread across many cities that store copies of websites so people can load them faster. Normally, a website lives on one machine called the origin server, which is the original computer holding all the real files. If everyone on Earth had to fetch data from that single machine, people far away would wait a long time for anything to appear. To fix this, copies of the site get stored on servers closer to where people actually are, called edge locations, since they sit at the edge of the network, nearer to homes and offices instead of far away in one data center. When someone requests a page and a nearby edge location already has a saved copy ready to hand over, that's called a cache hit, meaning the answer came from the nearby copy instead of a long trip back to the original machine. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries that each keep popular books on hand, so readers do not need to travel to one faraway central library every time. Fewer long trips mean pages load faster, websites survive sudden traffic surges better, and less strain falls on the original computer. This entire arrangement mostly happens invisibly in the background while people simply browse.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|------|---------------|-----------------|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's real files | Everything ultimately starts from here |
| Edge location | A nearby server holding a copy of the content | Shortens the distance data must travel |
| Cache hit | A request answered by a stored copy instead of the origin | Makes pages load noticeably faster |
| Content delivery network | The whole network of edge locations working together | Keeps websites fast and reliable worldwide |
